claims.text: Controlled annealing can promote nanoscale grain-boundary segregation in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Nanoscale grain-boundary segregation can create magnetic pinning sites.
Annealing-induced pinning sites will increase the coercive field of magnetic high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy is homogeneous and has a uniformly distributed grain structure.
Sub-critical annealing in an inert atmosphere can induce nanoscale grain-boundary segregation.
Sub-critical annealing can induce subtle disorder without significant grain growth or undesirable phase transformations.
The segregation features will remain metastable when annealing temperature and duration are appropriately controlled.
Nanoscale chemical segregation or disordered grain boundaries produce enhanced grain-boundary pinning sites.
Segregation-induced pinning centers impede magnetic-domain-wall motion.
Impeded magnetic-domain-wall motion increases coercive field relative to untreated, uniformly structured samples.
Controlled annealing will produce a statistically significant increase in coercive field relative to an untreated matched baseline.
The untreated baseline has minimal natural grain-boundary pinning effects.
The coercivity increase requires annealing mild enough to avoid large-scale grain growth or phase decomposition.
Overly aggressive annealing may reduce coercivity by eliminating fine-scale pinning sites.
There is no direct prior evidence in the provided dataset for the proposed intervention and mechanism.
The optimal annealing temperature, duration, and magnitude of coercivity increase are uncertain.
